## 1. Sharing and reusing data
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2024-11-25, over a year ago.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Sharing and reusing data](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/designing-with-data-an-introduction#sharing-and-reusing-data))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "You should consider how other teams may benefit from using the data you collect, so you can make it as reusable as possible."

Section text (verbatim):
> You should consider how other teams may benefit from using the data you collect, so you can make it as reusable as possible. In addition, your service may be better to use and easier to run if it gets data from other parts of government.
> Reusing existing data can:
> improve the quality of services by avoiding asking users for more information than is necessary
> save teams and users time and money
> avoid unnecessary duplication of data
> increase the efficiency of cyber security measures
> reduce the risk of errors and inconsistencies
> You can look for existing government data sets that you might be able to use to meet the needs of your service.
> Application programming interfaces (APIs) are another useful way to share and reuse data across services. An API is software that connects websites and mobile applications to databases so that they can exchange data, without giving direct access to the database. This exchange could be one way or reciprocal - other teams may benefit from using your data, too.
> The APIs in the API Catalogue are published by public sector organisations in the UK. You can use it to find and access inter-departmental data exchanges.
> If you are building your own API, follow the API technical and data standards and read the guidance on designing, building and managing APIs.

## 2. Reuse as much as possible > Reuse common components
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2021-09-29, over three years ago: verify it is still current.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Reuse common components](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/making-services-in-an-emergency#reuse-common-components))

Section text (verbatim):
> Using common components makes it easier to build user-centred services because you do not have to invent your own solutions to problems. For example, instead of each service team getting a payment provider, we’ve created one payment product that can be used by everyone.

## 3. 8. Designing effective contracts with common data standards > Contractual terms and conditions for cloud
Source: The Digital, Data and Technology Playbook (`ddat-playbook`), Digital, Data and Technology Profession. Authority: mandatory (comply or explain). page last updated 2023-06-20, over three years ago: verify it is still current.
Cite inline as: ([The Digital, Data and Technology Playbook: Contractual terms and conditions for cloud](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-digital-data-and-technology-playbook/the-digital-data-and-technology-playbook-html#contractual-terms-and-conditions-for-cloud))
**WARNING (SUPERSEDED, curated):** on who assures TCoP compliance and approves digital and technology spend, since 2026-04-01, this source is overtaken by "Getting approval to spend money on a service" (`spend-controls`). Treat the Service Manual as current on who approves digital and technology spend. The rest of the playbook, including its separate commercial spend control, is not affected by this.

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "Post EU Exit, contracting authorities should use the approved UK SCCs."
  - Possible conflict (machine-suggested, NOT verified): similar wording in "The Teal Book: Project delivery in government", pages about 3.3 years apart: "Contracting authorities should ensure they are familiar with the obligations set out in the Procurement Act 2023 as soon as they become aware they have to carry out a procurement." https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/home/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-25-procurement-and-contract-management/#:~:text=25.6.1.1%20Complying%20with%20the%20Procurement%20Act%202023,-The%20Procurement%20Act
- [RECOMMENDED] "This should operate on a “notice and veto” basis."
- [RECOMMENDED] "As detailed in PPN 05/16 open book contract management should be used."
- [RECOMMENDED] "For all of these factors, it is essential that the effect of critical government terms and conditions is maintained and contracting authorities should have a strategy in place for how supplier terms and conditions and any variations are managed."
  - Possible conflict (machine-suggested, NOT verified): similar wording in "The Teal Book: Project delivery in government", pages about 3.3 years apart: "Contracting authorities should ensure they are familiar with the obligations set out in the Procurement Act 2023 as soon as they become aware they have to carry out a procurement." https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/home/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-25-procurement-and-contract-management/#:~:text=25.6.1.1%20Complying%20with%20the%20Procurement%20Act%202023,-The%20Procurement%20Act
- [RECOMMENDED] "This should include transparency and financial monitoring requirements of the main supplier and critical subcontractors."
- [RECOMMENDED] "Issue logs should be kept of any unacceptable terms and conditions and/ or variances, and legal advice sought as appropriate."

Section text (verbatim):
> Contracting for cloud and SaaS can differ from how we contract for other products and services due to the one-to-many data model. There are a number of considerations often included in supplier terms and conditions for cloud contracts which contracting authorities will need to consider:
> Cloud and cyber security: Cloud service providers often require customers to contractually recognise their particular ‘shared responsibility models’ which set out predefined responsibilities around managing cyber security risk for both the customer and supplier.
> Data protection: Due to the multinational nature of supply chains, data may, in some instances, temporarily cross international borders. This will not constitute a breach of data protection requirements where data is only “in transit” (e.g. data is being transmitted over the Internet and certain packets transit through a network in a particular jurisdiction). The transfer of data to another jurisdiction will, however, always constitute a restricted transfer.
> GDPR: EU Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) are often incorporated into suppliers’ proprietary ‘data processing agreements’ by default to ensure the contract covers all eventualities. Post EU Exit, contracting authorities should use the approved UK SCCs. These are currently the same as the old EU SCCs but remember to check current requirements on this as the ICO is consulting on a refresh of UK SCCs.
> Cloud Subprocessors: Cloud service providers often require customers to provide an upfront “general written authorisation” for them to use new subprocessors, or third-party affiliates to undertake certain tasks. This should operate on a “notice and veto” basis. Existing subprocessors are more typically agreed expressly by consent.
> URL terms and conditions: Cloud and SaaS providers almost universally ask customers to include reference to service specific terms and conditions by way of URLs to their websites.
> As detailed in PPN 05/16 open book contract management should be used.
> For all of these factors, it is essential that the effect of critical government terms and conditions is maintained and contracting authorities should have a strategy in place for how supplier terms and conditions and any variations are managed. This should include transparency and financial monitoring requirements of the main supplier and critical subcontractors.
> Issue logs should be kept of any unacceptable terms and conditions and/ or variances, and legal advice sought as appropriate. Guidance will be developed by Cabinet Office and Crown Commercial
> Service to support contracting authorities to manage these considerations.

## 4. Deciding whether to use the cloud
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2024-10-17, over a year ago.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Deciding whether to use the cloud](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/securing-your-cloud-environment#deciding-whether-to-use-the-cloud))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [MANDATORY] "You must still do a risk analysis and mitigation exercise if you choose to use the public cloud."

Section text (verbatim):
> It’s government policy to use the public cloud first for almost all information classed as official and some sensitive data.
> Follow the Creating and implementing a cloud hosting strategy and the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) cloud security guidance to decide if cloud security meets your needs.
> To better analyse your service’s security risks, make sure you understand:
> your business requirements
> the information you want to store and where you want to store it
> if the cloud provider can give you enough assurance of their security measures
> what user and administrator security your organisations uses
> how you will monitor your security processes to make sure they are working
> You must still do a risk analysis and mitigation exercise if you choose to use the public cloud.
> Learn about government Secure by Design principles and managing third-party product security risks.

## 5. Finding a secure cloud provider
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2024-10-17, over a year ago.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Finding a secure cloud provider](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/securing-your-cloud-environment#finding-a-secure-cloud-provider))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "You should also choose your provider from a trusted place such as the Digital Marketplace or the Crown Commercial Service."

Section text (verbatim):
> Use the government’s Cloud Security Principles to help you evaluate cloud providers.
> You will need to identify which of the principles your service needs and find a supplier who meets those needs. If your chosen cloud provider can not meet a principle, check if your team can meet it instead.
> You should also choose your provider from a trusted place such as the Digital Marketplace or the Crown Commercial Service.
> As you identify your needs, you might find you have to balance several factors along with security. For example, balancing the risk of technical lock-in and contract flexibility with the provider can mean that you need to do less security work to get the service up and running as they have done it for you.

## 6. Reuse as much as possible > Reuse open standards
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2021-09-29, over three years ago: verify it is still current.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Reuse open standards](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/making-services-in-an-emergency#reuse-open-standards))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "share information between emergency services you should use MAIT (Multi Agency Incident Transfer) as the open standard to exchange information about incidents"
- [RECOMMENDED] "When the immediate crisis has passed and if you were unable to adopt some of the recommended standards, revisit your service journey or product specification to see what you should change."

Section text (verbatim):
> Use open standards as much as possible. This allows the service or product you’re designing to be interoperable from the outset so that it works seamlessly across government and the wider public and private sectors. Using an international open standard also makes it easier to exchange information.
> For example, if your service will:
> share information between emergency services you should use MAIT (Multi Agency Incident Transfer) as the open standard to exchange information about incidents
> refer people to other services, for example to tackle vulnerability issues at critical times such as in emergencies, use the OpenReferralUK standard
> If your service uses contact information like addresses, use the open standards for government data and technology. This will make it quicker to build your service and get it assessed.
> If you need help, contact the Data Standards Authority.
> When the immediate crisis has passed and if you were unable to adopt some of the recommended standards, revisit your service journey or product specification to see what you should change.
